title: My First Week at Work
subtitle: Four verbs that give learners trouble — say, tell, speak and talk — in a situation where you actually need them.
description: An A2 reading and listening text set during a first week at a new job, built around the difference between say, tell, speak and talk, with vocabulary and exercises.
passage: On my first day at the store, my manager told me to arrive at eight. I got there at ten to eight, because I did not want to be late on the first morning.

My manager's name is Diane. She said good morning, and then she talked to me for about twenty minutes about how the store works. She told me where the break room was, she told me when my lunch break was, and she said I could ask her anything at all.

Then she introduced me to Ray, who has worked there for nine years. Ray does not talk very much, but when he speaks, people listen. He said only one thing to me that morning: "Ask before you guess." I have thought about that a lot since then.

On Tuesday a customer asked me where the batteries were, and I had no idea. I remembered what Ray said, so I told the customer to wait one moment and I went and asked. She thanked me for checking instead of pointing her in the wrong direction.

On Wednesday Diane spoke to me about the register. I was slow, and I knew it. She did not say I was doing badly. She said, "You are careful, and careful is the right thing to be in your first week. Speed comes later."
By Friday I could talk to customers without feeling nervous. I still could not answer everything, but I had learned to say "Let me find out for you" instead of guessing.

On Friday evening, Diane told me I had done well. Then she said something I did not expect: "Next week you can start training the new person." I laughed and told her I had only been there five days. She said that was exactly why — I still remembered what was confusing.

vocabulary.definition: say + the words. You do not need a person: 'She said good morning.'
tell + a person. 'She told me where the break room was.'
slightly more formal than 'talk'; often about one serious thing
to have a conversation, usually informal and two-way
the room at work where employees eat and rest
the machine where customers pay (British English: the till)
to give an answer you are not sure about
to get information you do not have yet

exercises.title: Say, Tell, Speak or Talk?
exercises.instructions: Choose the correct verb. Remember: you tell a person, but you just say something.

items.prompt: Diane ___ me to arrive at eight.
items.explanation: 'Tell' takes a person straight after it: told me. 'Said me' is not possible in English.
'Say' is followed by the words, with no person: said good morning.

items.prompt: She ___ to me for twenty minutes about the store.
items.explanation: 'Talk to someone' describes a conversation. Note the preposition: talk TO me.

items.prompt: Ray does not ___ very much, but people listen when he does.
items.explanation: Here the verb has no object at all, so 'talk' is the natural choice.

items.prompt: On Wednesday Diane ___ to me about the register.
items.explanation: 'Speak to someone about something' is slightly more formal and suits a serious, one-topic conversation.

items.prompt: I ___ the customer to wait one moment.
items.explanation: Again a person follows directly: told the customer.

items.prompt: I learned to ___ "Let me find out for you."
items.explanation: The exact words follow, with no person, so 'say' is correct.

items.prompt: She ___ me I had done well.
items.explanation: 'Told me (that)...' — a person plus the information.

exercises.title: Understanding the Text
exercises.instructions: The questions use different words from the text. Think about the meaning, not the exact wording.

items.prompt: Why did the writer arrive before eight?
options: Diane asked him to come early
He wanted to be sure he was not late on day one
The store opened at ten to eight
items.explanation: “I did not want to be late on the first morning” — arriving early was his own caution.

items.prompt: What kind of person is Ray?
options: He talks a lot but says little
He says little, and people pay attention when he does
He is unfriendly to new staff
items.explanation: “Ray does not talk very much, but when he speaks, people listen.”

items.prompt: A customer asked about something he did not know. What did he do?
options: He asked her to wait and went to check
He sent her to another employee
items.explanation: He followed Ray's advice — ask before you guess — and went to find out.

options: She was annoyed at the delay
She was grateful he checked instead of guessing
items.explanation: “She thanked me for checking instead of pointing her in the wrong direction.”

items.prompt: Diane knew he was slow on the register. What did she choose to say about it?
options: That being careful matters more than being fast at first
That he needed to improve immediately
items.explanation: “You are careful, and careful is the right thing to be in your first week. Speed comes later.” She addressed it, but framed it as a strength.

items.prompt: Why is being new an advantage for training the next person, in Diane's view?
options: New staff have more free time
He still remembers which parts are confusing
items.explanation: “That was exactly why — I still remembered what was confusing.” Someone experienced has forgotten what was hard.

exercises.title: Find the Mistake
exercises.instructions: Each sentence has one mistake with say, tell, speak or talk. Write the corrected sentence.

items.incorrect: She said me to arrive at eight.
items.answer: She told me to arrive at eight.
items.explanation: 'Say' cannot take a person directly. Use 'told me', or 'said to me'.

items.incorrect: He told that the store was closed.
items.answer: He said that the store was closed.
items.explanation: 'Tell' needs a person: told me that... Without a person, use 'said that'.

items.incorrect: I talked her about the problem.
items.answer: I talked to her about the problem.
items.explanation: 'Talk' needs the preposition 'to' before the person.

items.incorrect: Can I speak you for a moment?
items.answer: Can I speak to you for a moment?

discussion: Describe your first day in a job, at a school, or in a new city. What did someone tell you that helped?
Ray says, "Ask before you guess." Is that good advice in your own work? Why or why not?
Diane praised him for being careful rather than fast. Which matters more when you are new at something?
Write about 70 words about someone who taught you something at work or at school. Use 'said', 'told me' and 'talked to me' at least once each.
